overview.text: Ivan Petrovich Pavlov (1849–1936) was a Russian physiologist whose experiments linked digestion with the nervous system. After beginning religious studies, he turned to science and investigated how digestive secretions worked. While studying dogs, Pavlov observed that salivation could begin before food arrived; he tested how a signal repeatedly paired with food could later trigger salivation on its own. He called this acquired response a “conditioned reflex,” distinguishing it from an unlearned reflex. This work helped make learned responses experimentally measurable and influenced the study of behavior. Pavlov received the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on digestion, not for the conditioning experiments.

key_facts.text: Pavlov was born in Ryazan in 1849, studied for the priesthood before pursuing science, and died in 1936.
His 1904 Nobel Prize recognized his research on the physiology of digestion.
His digestive research included methods for collecting secretions from different glands to study how they worked.
Pavlov called a learned response to a signal associated with food a “conditioned reflex”; he distinguished it from an unconditioned reflex.
His work helped establish experimental ways to investigate learned behavior and the relationship between behavior and bodily processes.
